newsitem.title: USA: IBM soars, Q1 shows new balance in revenue.
newsitem.headline: IBM soars, Q1 shows new balance in revenue.

text.p: Shares of International Business Machines Corp soared over seven percent in heavy trading after its first quarter impressed analysts with a healthier balance in its revenues and good cost controls.

Despite a big decline in its most profitable hardware lines, mainframes and the AS/400 minicomputer family, IBM managed to beat Wall Street consensus estimates with first quarter earnings of $2.37 a share, through faster growth in other businesses, expense controls and a lower tax rate.
Gary Helmig, a SoundView Financial analyst, said IBM demonstrated "exquisite financial management," in the quarter.
IBM's shares, which were delayed in opening, climbed to an intrasession high of 157, before falling back to 151-5/8 with a gain of 9-1/4. IBM was the most active issue on the NYSE.

"The company's point was that the strength of its portfolio of businesses is showing through," said Steve Milunovich, a Morgan Stanley analyst. "For example, the company was able to offset paltry mainframe MIPS (a measure of processing power shipped) growth of six percent with success in businesses such as hard disks...Inconsistencies in individual businesses net out for overall consistency."
He raised estimates slightly due to its lower tax rate.
Helmig of SoundView said that IBM is managing a difficult transition to lower-margin, faster growing businesses, from slower growing, higher profit margin businesses.

"They have had a tough transformation going on," Helmig said. "As the higher margin businesses are languishing, they are switching to lower margin, higher-growth business, yet they were able to get stockholder earnings growth."
Analysts said that IBM's expense controls offset the pressures on its sales profit margins, as its hardware gross profit margins fell to 32.4 percent of revenues, versus 35.1 percent a year ago.

Analysts cautioned that a strong dollar will continue to have a negative impact going forward this year, and one analyst, Andrew Neff at Bear Stearns, lowered his earnings estimates, based on the stronger dollar. In the first quarter, IBM said currency translations reduced earnings by $0.19 per share.

"There are some puts and takes for the year," said John Jones, a Salomon Brothers analyst. "Currency is going to be tougher than expected." But he added that IBM had every opportunity to guide Wall Street to lower estimates for the year, but its chief financial officer Richard Thoman said he was "comfortable" with analysts' current financial models.
IBM, however, said that any further negative impact from currency fluctuations will be offset by an expected lower tax rate and fewer shares outstanding, due to its stock buyback plan.
IBM's shares outstanding were reduced to 501.7 million, from 544.3 million a year ago, in the first quarter.
